# METHODOLOGY

This chapter explains how the study answers its research questions. It describes how the posts are collected and annotated, how the models are trained and compared, and how the benchmarking system and the prototype web application are built and tested.

## Research Methodology

This study follows the Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM) of Peffers et al. [-@peffers2007design]. Design science research creates and evaluates artifacts intended to solve identified problems [@peffers2007design]. DSRM is used because the main contribution of the study is an artifact, a multi-task model that performs humanitarian classification and NER on Taglish typhoon posts. The study also contributes a second artifact, a dataset of Taglish typhoon posts annotated for both tasks, on which the model is trained.

The study carries out the six activities of DSRM in order [@peffers2007design]. The first two activities, identifying the problem and defining the objectives of a solution, are presented in Chapter 1. In design and development, the dataset is built and the multi-task model is designed. The validation set is then used to select one of 13 multi-task optimizers, and the model trained with this optimizer becomes the final model. In demonstration, the final model is used in a prototype web application that performs humanitarian classification and NER on posts. In evaluation, the final model is compared on the test set with two single-task models, one for each task, and the agreement between the annotators is measured to evaluate the dataset. In communication, the results are reported in this thesis, and the final model, the code, and the post IDs of the dataset are released.

## Subjects of the Study

The subjects of this study are the dataset, the multi-task model, and the single-task models. The dataset and the multi-task model are the artifacts that the study contributes, whereas the single-task models are trained only as baselines for the multi-task model. The dataset comprises approximately 2,500 Taglish posts on X about the tropical cyclones of January to November 2026. Each post is annotated for both tasks, with one of the ten humanitarian categories of HumAID [@alam2021humaid] for humanitarian classification (@tbl-categories) and with entity spans of the ten entity types of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner] for NER (@tbl-entity-types). The eleventh label of HumAID, which is for posts that an annotator cannot judge, is omitted, as in HUMAID-NER. Both schemes are adopted because HUMAID-NER applies them to the same disaster posts [@ali2026humaidner], so the results of this study can be compared with those of HUMAID-NER.

The multi-task model adopts hard parameter sharing (@fig-artifact), in which two task heads, one for humanitarian classification and one for NER, share a single pretrained transformer encoder. This design is widely used [@vandenhende2022dense] and is also the design of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. The encoder is SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, which is chosen because it was pretrained on 13 languages, including English and Filipino [@aisingapore2026sealion]. Both task heads and their cross-entropy losses follow HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. Training the multi-task model with each of the 13 multi-task optimizers in @tbl-optimizers yields 13 candidate models.

The 13 optimizers are selected using two criteria. First, each must have been evaluated in at least two of the seven empirical studies of multi-task optimizers reviewed in Chapter 2. This criterion limits the comparison to well-established optimizers, following Kurin et al. [-@kurin2022unitary]. Second, each must be trainable with the same model and training setup as the others, so that the optimizer is the only difference among the candidate models. The 13 optimizers in @tbl-optimizers are the only ones that meet both criteria.

Each single-task model uses the same encoder as the candidate models and the same task head and loss for its task, but it is trained on that task alone. In total, 15 models are trained, the 13 candidate models and the two single-task models.

## Sampling Technique

The sampling frame consists of the posts on X that match the search keywords and fall within the collection window of a tropical cyclone. Each window runs from one day before to three days after the period during which the tropical cyclone was within the Philippine Area of Responsibility, based on the dates in the preliminary tropical cyclone reports of PAGASA [-@pagasa2026prelim]. The window extends beyond this period because people also post about a tropical cyclone before it arrives and after it leaves. Zou et al. [-@zou2025typhoon] likewise collected posts from two days before to four days after landfall. The extension is shorter in this study because the period within the Philippine Area of Responsibility already includes the days of approach. Overlapping windows are merged so that each post enters the frame only once.

The search keywords are *bagyo* (tropical cyclone), *baha* (flood), and words formed from these two Tagalog roots, such as *bagyong* and *pagbaha* (@tbl-keyword-forms). The two roots refer to the hazard itself and to flooding, one of its effects in the Philippines [@ermino2022urgency]. Every word form is searched as a separate keyword because the search function of X matches a keyword as a token of the post, so a root is not expected to match the longer words formed from it [@x2026operators]. Storm names are not used as keywords, because many local storm names are also personal names and match far more posts than the keywords do (@tbl-storm-names).

A post is included when it contains at least one English word and at least one Tagalog word. The language of each word is identified with the dictionary-based method of Herrera et al. [-@herrera2022tweettaglish], which labels a word as English, Tagalog, or other. This method is used because it was developed for Taglish posts on the same platform. A requirement higher than one word of each language is not set, because it would need an arbitrary cutoff.

Reposts and quotes are excluded. A repost repeats a post that is already in the frame, and a quote includes text written by another user. Exact and near duplicates are also excluded, because repeated text would be counted more than once and could appear in both the training set and the test set. A near duplicate is a post whose text matches that of another post except for small changes. Duplicates are identified with the method of HumAID [@alam2021humaid]. Links, usernames, and non-ASCII characters are first removed, so that posts differing only in these elements are treated as identical. Each post is then represented by the counts of its words and word pairs, and the cosine similarity between the counts of two posts measures how much wording the two posts share. When this similarity exceeds 0.75, only one of the two posts is kept. HumAID adopted this threshold from @alam2021crisisbench, who set it after manually checking posts at several thresholds.

About 2,500 posts are drawn for annotation by proportionate stratified random sampling, in which each day is a stratum that contributes posts in proportion to its number of matching posts. Simple random sampling is not used because it requires the full list of matching posts, which is too costly to retrieve. The number of matching posts on each day, in contrast, is available without retrieving the posts. The sample size is based on resource constraints [@lakens2022sample]. About 2,500 posts is the most that two annotators can complete at 2 to 3 hours a day over the 38 working days from December 2026 to January 2027.

The annotated posts are divided into a training set (72%), a validation set (14%), and a test set (14%), following the proportions of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. Every model uses the same split, so that differences between models cannot arise from differences in the posts. The split is stratified by humanitarian category, so each category has approximately the same share in all three sets.

## Instruments to Be Used

The study uses four measures. Cohen's kappa measures how well the two annotators agree, the F1-score measures how correctly a model performs each task, the relative change in F1-score measures negative transfer, and training time and peak memory measure training cost.

Inter-annotator agreement on the humanitarian categories is measured with Cohen's kappa [@cohen1960coefficient]. Two annotators can assign the same category to some posts by chance alone, so kappa corrects the proportion of posts on which the annotators agree for the agreement expected by chance. A kappa of 1 means complete agreement, and a kappa of 0 means no more agreement than chance. A high kappa indicates that the annotators apply the annotation guidelines in Appendix B consistently. No agreement is computed for the entity spans, because GLiNER [@zaratiana2024gliner] annotates them automatically.

Model performance refers to how correctly a model assigns humanitarian categories and marks entity spans. It is evaluated with the F1-score, as in HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner], by comparing the predictions of a model with the annotated categories and the GLiNER spans. Accuracy is not used, because the categories differ in their number of posts and a model can reach a high accuracy by favoring the most frequent categories. The F1-score combines two proportions, precision and recall. Precision is the proportion of the predictions of a model that are correct, and recall is the proportion of the annotated items that the model finds. For a humanitarian category or an entity type $c$,
$$P_c = \frac{TP_c}{TP_c + FP_c}, \qquad R_c = \frac{TP_c}{TP_c + FN_c}, \qquad F1_c = \frac{2 P_c R_c}{P_c + R_c}$$
where $TP_c$ is the number of correct predictions of $c$, $FP_c$ is the number of incorrect predictions of $c$, $FN_c$ is the number of instances of $c$ that the model fails to predict, and $P_c$ and $R_c$ are precision and recall. An F1-score of 1 means that every prediction is correct and no annotated item is missed.

Humanitarian classification is scored with macro-F1, the mean of $F1_c$ over the ten categories, which gives rare categories the same weight as frequent ones. NER is scored with span-level micro-F1, which pools the counts of all ten entity types before the formula is applied. A predicted span counts as correct only when both its boundaries and its type match those of an annotated span. Both scores are computed as in HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner], which allows them to be compared with the scores reported there.

Negative transfer occurs when a multi-task model has a lower F1-score on a task than the model trained on that task alone. It is measured as the relative change in F1-score from the single-task model, a widely used measure of multi-task performance [@vandenhende2022dense; @gama2026uniform]. The relative change shows by what percentage the F1-score of a candidate model is higher or lower than that of the single-task model. It is computed for each task $t$ and averaged over the two tasks,
$$\Delta_t = \frac{F1_{\text{multi-task},\,t} - F1_{\text{single-task},\,t}}{F1_{\text{single-task},\,t}} \times 100\%, \qquad \Delta_{\text{MTL}} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\Delta_1 + \Delta_2\right)$$
where task 1 is humanitarian classification and task 2 is NER. Here, $F1_{\text{multi-task},\,t}$ is the F1-score of one run of a candidate model, and $F1_{\text{single-task},\,t}$ is the mean F1-score over the five runs of the single-task model for task $t$. The mean is used because studies of multi-task optimizers compare each multi-task result with one single-task result for each task [@navon2022bargaining; @liu2023famo]. For example, when a candidate model reaches an F1-score of 0.76 on a task and the single-task model reaches 0.80, $\Delta_t$ is −5%. A negative $\Delta_t$ indicates negative transfer on task $t$, and a positive $\Delta_t$ indicates positive transfer.

Training time is the time, in seconds, that a run spends on training steps. Peak memory is the largest amount of graphics processing unit (GPU) memory, in mebibytes, that PyTorch allocates at any moment of the run. Because one multi-task model replaces both single-task models, it is compared with the two single-task models taken as a pair. The training time of the pair is the sum of the two training times. The peak memory of the pair is the larger of the two peak memories, because the single-task models are trained one after the other. The overhead of an optimizer is the percentage by which the training time or peak memory of its candidate model exceeds that of equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary; @liu2023famo].

## Procedure of Data Gathering

Posts are collected through the X API, which charges US\$0.005 for each post that it returns, including posts that are later excluded [@x2026pricing]. The keywords match 176,424 posts in the collection windows (@tbl-frame-counts), so retrieving all of them would cost about US\$882. To avoid this cost, only the number of matching posts on each day is requested first, and these numbers set the share of each day in the sample. The posts of each day are then retrieved and filtered by the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Retrieval within a day starts at times drawn at random, so that the retrieved posts are not only the latest posts of that day. Retrieval continues until the share of the day is filled. When a day has too few eligible posts to fill its share, the remainder is divided among the other days, and a day with more matching posts receives more of it. At US\$0.005 for each post, the 2,500 posts cost at least US\$12.50, and the final cost depends on how many of the retrieved posts are eligible. @tbl-collection-steps lists the steps of collection.

Users of X keep ownership of their posts but grant X a license to make the posts available to others [@x2026terms], so consent is not sought from each user. In the collected posts, usernames, phone numbers, email addresses, and links are replaced with placeholders, because these details can identify a person and are not needed for either task. Names within the text of a post are kept, because PERSON is one of the entity types. The posts are stored only on the laptop used for training, and only the research group and the adjudicator have access to them, in line with the Data Privacy Act [-@philippines2012dataprivacy]. As the developer policy of X requires, posts deleted on X are also deleted from the dataset, and only the post IDs are shared [@x2026devpolicy].

The humanitarian category of every post is assigned by two annotators, who work in the annotation tool doccano from December 2026 to January 2027. Both are members of the research group and are fluent in Tagalog and English, the two languages that the posts mix. Disagreements that the annotators cannot settle are decided by an adjudicator, who comes from outside the research group and works or does research in disaster management or crisis informatics. @tbl-annotators lists the qualifications and tasks of the annotators and the adjudicator.

Annotation begins with practice batches of 50 posts. These posts are collected in the same way as the sample but are not part of it, so that no post in the sample is seen before the guidelines are fixed. The guidelines are revised after each practice batch until Cohen's kappa reaches at least .61, the lower bound of substantial agreement [@landis1977measurement]. A practice batch takes less than one day at the planned pace of about 66 posts a day, so several rounds can be completed before the sample is annotated.

The guidelines are then fixed, and the sample is annotated in eight batches of about 310 posts, following the rules in @tbl-annotation-rules. At the planned pace, one batch is about one working week of annotation, so agreement is measured every week. Kappa is computed for each batch from the annotations that the two annotators make independently, before any discussion. When the kappa of a batch falls below .61, the annotators review the guidelines and their disagreements with the adjudicator before the next batch begins. The batch is not annotated again, because the 38 working days leave no time to repeat it.

After kappa is computed, the annotators settle their disagreements by discussion. The adjudicator decides the disagreements that remain and signs off on the batch. The adjudicator has the final decision because a disagreement that remains after discussion is one that neither the guidelines nor the annotators could settle, and the adjudicator has more knowledge of disaster response than the annotators.

The entity spans are not annotated manually, because marking every span takes considerably longer than choosing one category, and the available annotation time covers only the categories. The automatic annotation pipeline of HUMAID-NER is not used either, because it relies on an English language model and on rules written for English [@ali2026humaidner]. The spans are instead marked by GLiNER [@zaratiana2024gliner], a pretrained NER model whose multilingual version suits posts that mix two languages. GLiNER is used in zero-shot mode, in which it receives the ten entity types as its labels and is not trained on any post of the study. It is run with its default confidence threshold of 0.5 (@tbl-gliner-settings). It is applied after the placeholders are inserted, so that usernames are not marked as entities and GLiNER reads the same text as the models.

The models are trained on the training set with LibMTL [@lin2023libmtl], a library that provides 12 of the 13 optimizers. The thirteenth, linear scalarization, is implemented for this study. @tbl-training-settings lists the training settings, and @tbl-optimizer-setup lists how each optimizer is set up. Every model is trained for 10 epochs, each of which is one pass over the training set [@warner2025modernbert]. After each epoch, the model is scored on the validation set, and the version of the model from the epoch with the highest validation score is kept [@kurin2022unitary]. For a multi-task model, the validation score is the mean of its two F1-scores, and for a single-task model, it is the F1-score of its task, following HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner]. Early stopping, which ends training once the validation score stops rising, is not used, because a comparison of multi-task optimizers should give every model the same amount of training [@xin2022mtohelp]. The batch size is 8, and the embedding layer of the encoder, which holds 201 million of its 312 million parameters, is not trained in any model. Both settings allow every optimizer to fit in the 8 GB of GPU memory of the laptop.

The learning rate, which sets the size of each update to a model, is tuned for each model, as in the reviewed comparisons of multi-task optimizers [@xin2022mtohelp; @kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform]. Each model is trained once with random seed 0 at each of the learning rates 1, 3, 5, and 8 × 10^−5^ [@warner2025modernbert], and the rate with the highest validation score is kept [@kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform]. For linear scalarization, the task weights are tuned together with the learning rate. At each learning rate, the weight of humanitarian classification is set to 0.1, 0.2, …, 0.9 and the weight of NER to one minus that value [@xin2022mtohelp; @royer2023scalarization].

Each model is then trained in five main runs with random seeds 1 to 5. Five runs fall within the range of two to ten runs used in the reviewed comparisons of multi-task optimizers [@kurin2022unitary; @lin2023libmtl; @royer2023scalarization]. A random seed fixes the random choices of a run, so runs with the same seed process the training posts in the same order, regardless of the model. Because training time is one of the measures, the order of the tuning runs and the order of the main runs are randomized, so that changes in the condition of the laptop over time do not favor any optimizer.

Because a sample size based on resource constraints may not be large enough [@lakens2022sample], each single-task model is also trained on 25%, 50%, and 75% of the training set. The resulting learning curve shows how the F1-scores change as more training posts are used [@tabuzo2026phmartiallawner]. The single-task models are used because each learns one task alone, so the curve is not affected by the choice of multi-task optimizer. Each smaller part is a random subset of the next larger part and preserves the proportions of the humanitarian categories, so that the parts differ only in size. A model is trained on each part with seeds 1 to 5 and with the learning rate tuned on the full training set.

## Statistical Treatment

Each result is reported as the mean and sample standard deviation across the five main runs of a model. The first research question is answered with the F1-scores of the single-task models on the test set. The second is answered with the dataset and the multi-task model themselves, together with the Cohen's kappa of each batch of annotation. The third is answered with the F1-scores, relative changes, training time, and peak memory of the 13 candidate models. The F1-scores and relative changes of the candidate models are computed on the validation set, because the test set is reserved for the final model and the single-task models.

The final model is also selected on the validation set. For each of the 13 candidate models, $\Delta_{\text{MTL}}$ is averaged over the five runs, and the optimizer of the candidate model with the highest mean becomes the optimizer of the final model. Among the five runs of the final model, the run with the highest validation score is used in the prototype and in the error analysis.

The fourth research question is answered on the test set, where the final model is compared with the single-task models. The hypotheses of Chapter 1 are tested with a two-sided paired t-test on the F1-scores, conducted once for each task. This test is appropriate because the hypotheses compare the means of two sets of F1-scores that form pairs. The runs are paired by random seed, so that each run of the final model is compared with the single-task run that processed the training posts in the same order. The test examines whether the mean of the five differences in F1-score is zero, and the null hypothesis is rejected when $p$ is below .05. The mean difference is reported with its 95% confidence interval. Training time and peak memory are compared through their means and standard deviations, without a statistical test.

## Data Analysis

The learning curve is used to judge whether the 2,500 posts are sufficient. It is interpreted by comparing adjacent training sizes, following Tabuzo et al. [-@tabuzo2026phmartiallawner], who considered a training size sufficient once a larger size no longer produced a significant gain in F1-score. This study compares the two largest sizes, 75% and 100% of the training set, because this step shows whether the F1-scores are still rising when the whole training set is used. The increase in the mean F1-score on the validation set from 75% to 100% is counted as a gain when it exceeds the standard deviation of the single-task model across its five main runs, which represents the usual variation between runs. An increase above this standard deviation indicates that more posts would likely raise the F1-scores further, and this result is reported as a limitation. A smaller increase indicates that the F1-scores have stopped improving and that the 2,500 posts are sufficient. The curve of each task is interpreted separately, and the limitation is reported for each task whose F1-score is still improving.

The F1-scores of the final model are interpreted through their difference from those of the single-task models. No minimum acceptable F1-score is set, because no earlier study reports F1-scores for both tasks on Taglish posts about tropical cyclones. The errors of the final model are then analyzed to show which posts it misinterprets and why. The analysis covers the predictions on the test set from the run that is used in the prototype. No difficult posts are deliberately added to the test set, so the errors reflect the kinds of posts that the model is meant to label. For humanitarian classification, a confusion matrix shows how often each category is mistaken for each of the other categories. For NER, each incorrect span is classified by entity type and by type of error, which is a missed span, an extra span, or a span with incorrect boundaries or an incorrect type. The posts with errors are then examined together to identify what they have in common, such as their length, their mix of Tagalog and English, or their category.

## Software System Description

The software system of this study has two parts, a benchmarking system that prepares the dataset and trains, selects, and evaluates the models, and a prototype web application that runs the final model.

### System Structure

![System Architecture of the Benchmarking System and the Prototype Web Application](figures/fig-3-1-system-architecture.pdf){#fig-system-architecture}

@fig-system-architecture is read from top to bottom. Its first two phases, data preparation and model training and selection, make up the benchmarking system, and the third phase is the prototype web application. The cylinders are stored data, and the slanted boxes are the input and output of the whole system.

The prototype has three parts, all of which run on the computer of the study, so the posts that the staff of a Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (DRRMO) analyze are not sent to an outside service. The interface, built with React, runs in a web browser and shows the posts, filters, summaries, and forms that the staff use. The server, built with FastAPI in Python, receives the requests from the interface, runs the final model with PyTorch to analyze new posts, and prepares the summaries and reports. The requests that the server accepts, such as a request to analyze a post, are described in an API specification that FastAPI generates in the standard OpenAPI format, and the specification is kept in the GitHub repository with the code. The database, PostgreSQL, stores the posts, their predicted and corrected labels, and their status.

### Use Cases

@fig-use-cases shows the actors of the prototype web application and their use cases. DRRMO staff are the main actor, and X is a secondary actor that supplies posts when the staff collect them directly. The researcher loads the trained model into the prototype and collects the labels that the staff correct. @tbl-usecases groups the use cases into five categories and describes each one and its result.

![Use Case Diagram of the Prototype Web Application](figures/fig-3-2-use-cases.pdf){#fig-use-cases}

| Use Case Category | Use Case | Description | Result |
|:----------------|:----------------|:------------------------------|:--------------------|
| Data input | Import posts | Loads a file of collected posts, or collects new posts from X using keywords and a date range set by the staff | The posts are stored in the database, ready to be analyzed |
| Classification and extraction | Analyze posts | Assigns one humanitarian category to each post and marks its entities with the trained multi-task model | Each post has a stored category and stored entity spans |
| Classification and extraction | View analyzed posts | Shows each post with its category and its entities highlighted | The staff see each post with its category and its entities highlighted |
| Classification and extraction | Correct a label | Lets the staff fix a wrong category or entity span | The corrected category or entity span replaces the predicted one and is saved as a correction |
| Monitoring | Filter posts | Shows only the posts of selected categories (such as requests or urgent needs), entity types, or dates | Only the posts that match the selected filters are shown |
| Monitoring | Mark post status | Marks a post as reviewed, forwarded to a response team, or not actionable | The new status of the post is saved |
| Reporting | View summary | Shows the number of posts per category and per location over time | The counts of posts per category and per location are shown over time |
| Reporting | Export report | Saves the filtered posts and summary counts as a file for situation reports | A CSV file of the filtered posts and summary counts is saved |
| Model management | Load trained model | Loads the final model into the prototype | The prototype uses the loaded model for every new analysis |
| Model management | Export corrected labels | Saves the labels corrected by the staff as a file that can be used to train future models | A JSON Lines file of the corrected posts is saved in the same format as the dataset |

## Testing and Evaluation

Testing checks that the software of the study works as designed. The benchmarking system is tested so that its scores and measurements are computed correctly, and the prototype is tested so that each use case works.

Testing moves from the smallest parts of the software to the whole system. Each part of the benchmarking code is tested first, then the whole benchmarking system, then the trained models, and finally the prototype. All tests run on the laptop in @tbl-hardware. The usability of the prototype, its use by DRRMO staff, and its performance on other computers are not tested. The benchmarking code is tested automatically with pytest, so that every test can be run again after any change to the code, and the prototype is tested by hand with written test cases. @tbl-tests summarizes what each test covers and when each test passes.

| Test | Item tested | Method | Pass criterion |
|:----------------|:--------------------|:--------------------|:--------------------|
| *Benchmarking system* | | | |
| Unit testing | Each part of the benchmarking code | Automated tests on hand-worked examples | Output matches the hand-worked result |
| Integration testing | Benchmarking system with all 15 models | Automated run on a small part of the data | Every model finishes and writes its result file |
| Performance testing | Best runs of the final and single-task models | Batches of 1, 16, and 32 posts | N/A |
| *Prototype* | | | |
| Functional testing | Each of the 10 use cases | Written test cases | Actual result matches the expected result in every test case |

: Test Summary {#tbl-tests tbl-colwidths="[20,28,26,26]"}

Note. The results of the performance testing are only described, so no pass criterion is set.

Before the tuning runs start, each part of the benchmarking code goes through unit testing, in which the part is run with pytest on small examples whose correct output is worked out by hand (Appendix E). The unit tests cover the placement of the NER label of each word on its first token, the scoring code, the 13 multi-task optimizers, the dataset split, and the order in which the training posts are shown. For example, one test checks that PCGrad leaves two task gradients unchanged when they do not conflict [@yu2020pcgrad], and another checks that Nash-MTL changes its task weights during training [@navon2022bargaining], as their original papers describe. Once every part passes, integration testing runs the whole benchmarking system for all 15 models on a small part of the data, from training to the result file of each run, which contains the settings, scores, and measurements of the run. This test passes when every model finishes and writes its result file. When any unit or integration test fails, the code is fixed and all the tests are run again, and the tuning runs start only after every test passes.

After the main runs, the final model and each single-task model go through performance testing, which measures how fast they label posts under different loads, since the prototype may receive one post at a time or a whole file of posts. Each model is tested with its main run that has the highest validation score, which for the final model is its prototype run. Each of these runs labels the test posts in batches of 1, 16, and 32 posts. A batch of 1 represents a single post, and the batches of 16 and 32 are larger than the batch size of 8 used in training. For each batch size, the processing time, which is the mean time taken to label one post, and the peak GPU memory are recorded. The processing time of the single-task models is the sum for the two models, since both must label each post. These results are only described.

Once the prototype is built, functional testing checks each of the 10 use cases in @tbl-usecases with at least one test case. Each test case states an input, the expected result, and the actual result (Appendix F). A use case passes when the actual result matches the expected result in every test case. When a test case fails, the prototype is fixed and every test case of that use case is run again.

@tbl-roles assigns each part of the study, including testing, to a member of the research group.

| Part of the study | Member | Responsibilities |
|:--------------------|:--------------------|:------------------------------|
| Data collection | \[To be assigned\] | Collection of posts through the X API |
| Cleaning | \[To be assigned\] | Removal of exact and near-duplicate posts and stratified sampling |
| Annotation | \[To be assigned\] | Annotation guidelines, batches, and agreement between the annotators |
| Benchmark code | \[To be assigned\] | Training and scoring code, the optimizers, and the unit and integration tests |
| Prototyping | \[To be assigned\] | The prototype web application and its use cases |
| Testing | \[To be assigned\] | Performance testing and functional testing |

: Researcher Roles {#tbl-roles tbl-colwidths="[25,25,50]"}
